decisions.title: Permission Check Before Every Tool Execution
decisions.description: Every tool call passes through a permission gate before execution. The gate normalizes the raw tool call into a structured intent (action type, target, risk level), then applies a policy pipeline: deny first, then check mode restrictions, then allow if safe, and ask the user as a last resort. This centralizes all safety logic in one place rather than scattering permission checks across individual tool handlers.
decisions.alternatives: Embedding permission logic in each tool handler is simpler initially but leads to inconsistent safety enforcement. A single global allow/deny boolean is too coarse for real-world use cases where some operations need confirmation and others are always safe.

decisions.title: The deny / mode / allow / ask Pipeline
decisions.description: Permission decisions follow a fixed pipeline order: (1) deny -- hard-blocked actions that should never execute, (2) mode -- session-level mode restrictions (read-only, plan-only), (3) allow -- auto-approved actions based on configured allowlists, (4) ask -- prompt the user for confirmation. This order ensures the most restrictive checks run first, so an action can never bypass a deny through a later allow rule.
decisions.alternatives: A single allowlist + blocklist is simpler but cannot express mode-based restrictions. An ACL-style system (access control lists per resource) is more granular but overkill for an agent's tool-level permissions.

decisions.title: Permission Results Become Visible Context
decisions.description: When permission is denied or the user is prompted, the result is written back into the conversation as a structured message. The model can see what happened ('permission denied: writing to /etc/hosts is not allowed') and reason about next steps. This makes permission outcomes part of the agent's visible state, not silent failures.
decisions.alternatives: Silent denial (drop the tool call without explanation) is simpler but leaves the model confused about why its action didn't happen. Raising an exception works but mixes control flow with safety policy.
